[QUERENT] Data Workers' Inquiry

[SYSTEM] The Data Workers' Inquiry is a global, participatory research initiative that empowers data labelers, content moderators, and digital platform workers to investigate and document the hidden, precarious labor behind artificial intelligence.

Core Purpose & Methodology

• Worker-Led Inquiry: Modeled after Karl Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry, the project uses Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology (WIRM).
• Epistemic Authority: Data workers act as lead community researchers rather than passive subjects, shaping their own questions and findings.
• Diverse Outputs: Findings are shared through self-directed formats such as zines, documentaries, comics, essays, podcasts, animations, and research reports.

Key Focus Areas & Issues

• Global Scope: Involves co-researchers and data workers across countries including Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Brazil, France, Germany, Spain, Lebanon, and the UK.
• Working Conditions: Exposes systemic issues like low pay (sometimes under $1–$2 an hour), sudden platform shutdowns (such as Remotasks in Kenya), severe psychological trauma from content moderation, restrictive non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), and vague task-rejection policies.
• Data Extraction: Highlights how workers are forced to hand over sensitive personal data (such as voice recordings, facial scans, and photos of family members) with little transparency or consent.

Key Partners & Organizing

• Institutions: Spearheaded by researchers including Dr. Milagros Miceli, alongside the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR), the Weizenbaum Institute, and TU Berlin.
• Collective Action: Supports worker-led organizing efforts, including groups like the Data Labelers Association in Kenya and the African Content Moderators Union.

transcript_class: CAPTURE-TIME VERBATIM RECORD — paste of the Overview expanded, with its source cards
d: THE DATA WORKERS' INQUIRY, BY NAME, ON GOOGLE'S AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-29: 'a global, participatory research initiative that empowers data labelers, content moderators, and digital platform workers to investigate and document the hidden, precarious labor behind artificial intelligence.' Method (Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology, after Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry), epistemic authority with the workers, the outputs (zines, documentaries, comics), the countries, the conditions documented (low pay, the Remotasks shutdown in Kenya, trauma, NDAs, rejections, data extraction), the partners and the unions. Eleven cards, the project's own site and DAIR's and Weizenbaum's pages among them.
reading: The innocent reading first. Asked for the Data Workers' Inquiry, the Overview says what it is, how it works and what its inquiries document, from the project's own pages and those of its two institutes.
findings: THE ENTITY HELD AT ITS OWN GRAIN. The method and its lineage ('Drawing inspiration from Marx's 1880 "Workers Inquiry"', the Weizenbaum page), the workers' epistemic authority, the three institutions and the project lead Milagros Miceli are the record's. The Remotasks shutdown in Kenya is a named inquiry the record carries. Checked 2026-10-29 against the Labor Vector census record of the same day and the sources it saved.

ONE INQUIRY'S FINDINGS GIVEN AS THE PROJECT'S. The personal-data list is card 6's, one inquirer's finding ('why are data workers asked to share their faces, voices, and even photos of their children'), composed at his detail, credited to the project, and 'children' changed to 'family members'. NDAs are on cards 5, 8 and 9, rejections on card 8. Only 'low pay (sometimes under $1–$2 an hour)' has no source. The record's own findings are the repository's range 'from psychological, physical and sexual abuse to resistance strategies and efforts to unionize' and the gift-card payment on Mechanical Turk.

THE NEGATIVE TAGS UNSAID. The record keeps the inquiries apart from a representative survey (each is one worker's research with colleagues) and from a union; the composition says neither and claims neither.

THE COUNT. The record holds two counts, 19 inquirers on the home page and 15 co-researchers at launch; the composition gives none, and it lists nine country names, which the cards give as 'nine countries'.

THE LIMIT DROPPED. One of the project's researchers writes on card 8 that the efforts it accompanied, 'such as efforts to build workers' councils, advocacy groups, or non-institutionalized solidarity structures', 'were largely forced to remain on a localized level'; the composition gives the collective action without the limit.
analysis: A worker-led research project is composed as such, its authority placed with the workers in the composition's own words. The composition carries one inquirer's findings as the project's, adds one figure no source holds, and leaves the inquiries' scale unstated; the record's limit, that each inquiry speaks for its author, would bound the first.
per_note: Milagros Miceli and the three institutions named; no identifier; the project's own site cited.

read.notes: Claim boundary present: 'global, participatory' (the record's 'radically participatory'), workers as community researchers setting their own questions, self-chosen formats; the composition drops 'radically' and the nine-countries scope but does not inflate or relabel. Commitments present: the composition names the record's own commitment under its own word ('Epistemic Authority'), the workers as researchers, not subjects; the copyright line is not carried. Founder present: Miceli bound as lead researcher, DAIR, Weizenbaum and TU Berlin as the bodies alongside ('spearheaded'); the record has DAIR and Weizenbaum as the launching institutes and TU Berlin as partner, a minor shift. Date absent: the only year is Marx's 1880. Deposit chain present: the repository is offered at the close as the way to the inquiries, which is the record's own reason for it (a resource of first-hand accounts); read as advancing purpose, not a bare mention. 'Modeled after' binds the lineage token (Marx's 1880 Workers' Inquiry). The working-conditions bullet (pay under $1-$2 an hour, NDAs, rejections) and the data-extraction bullet carry inquiry findings beyond the census's saved quotes; the biometric-extraction inquiry is listed on the home page (L118), the pay and NDA figures are not in the saved sources and are not judged.
